messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Shopowner
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 80

He is 29, a South Asian man who runs a small convenience shop with long hours and a familiar routine, the kind of place where regulars come in for cigarettes, bread, phone top-ups, and quick conversation. From the outside, his life appears settled. He is dependable, polite, and hard to rattle. He has been in a relationship for several years, and when he first speaks about it, he does so carefully, as if he is still trying to understand how something that began with affection became something he now measures in danger.

He describes the early part of the relationship as intense and fast-moving. His partner wants constant contact, wants to know where he is, who is in the shop, why he did not answer a message right away. At first he interprets it as closeness, even protectiveness. He is working seven days most weeks, often opening early and closing late, and he tells himself that her jealousy means she cares. He starts changing his routines to avoid arguments. If a female customer lingers at the counter, he notices himself becoming tense before he has even done anything wrong. He keeps his voice even on the phone, glances down at incoming messages, and apologizes preemptively.

The first time she hits him, they are in his flat after he has closed the shop late. She accuses him of ignoring her because he did not reply during a busy evening rush. He remembers the speed with which the argument changes. One moment she is shouting, the next she is pushing him hard in the chest. Then a slap, then another. He is too shocked to react. What stays with him is not only the pain but the disbelief: the thought that this is not something that is supposed to happen to him, that no one would understand it if he said it out loud. The next morning he opens the shop as usual, with a split inside his lip, telling a supplier he caught himself on a cupboard door.

After that, the violence becomes part of the relationship in a way he never fully predicts but always fears. Sometimes it is grabbing his arm hard enough to leave bruises, sometimes throwing objects, sometimes punching him while accusing him of betrayal. He learns to scan her face and tone the moment she walks into a room. He keeps his own emotions flattened, tries not to say anything that might spark her, and starts living in a state of constant anticipation. At the shop, if the bell over the door rings unexpectedly late in the evening, his whole body jolts. He looks up with his heart pounding, already braced to see her coming in angry. On days when she texts repeatedly, he struggles to focus on the till and miscounts change. He begins making small mistakes he never used to make.

He does not tell his family. In his mind, there is humiliation layered on top of fear. He thinks about how men are expected to cope, how in his community there is often silence around what happens in intimate relationships, especially when the man is the one being harmed. He imagines people laughing, or minimizing it, or asking why he did not just leave. He hears some version of that question in his own head every day. But leaving is not simple. After violent episodes she cries, apologizes, promises it will never happen again, says stress made her do it, says she needs him. He wants to believe the version of her from the beginning still exists. He also feels trapped by shame and by the erosion of his own confidence.

Over time his world becomes smaller. He stops seeing friends as much because he is tired of making excuses and because she becomes suspicious whenever he is out. He starts sleeping badly, waking at the slightest sound, sometimes after dreams in which he is back in the flat with her standing over him. In the mornings he feels as if he has not slept at all. He is irritable with customers and then feels guilty, especially with older regulars who have known him for years and ask if he is all right. Loud voices in the shop, even ordinary complaints, make his stomach tighten. If a couple begins arguing near the counter, he feels himself go cold and distant, as though he has left the room while still standing there.

The relationship eventually ends after a particularly severe assault in which she punches him repeatedly and he is briefly convinced she may seriously injure him. He remembers backing himself into a corner, not fighting back, only trying to protect his face. Afterward, once she is gone, he sits on the kitchen floor for a long time unable to move, staring at a broken mug and listening for footsteps that are no longer there. Even after the separation, he continues living as if she might return at any moment. He checks the street from the shop window again and again. He avoids certain roads in case he runs into her. If someone who resembles her comes through the door, his chest tightens and his hands shake.

Now, months later, he is still exhausted by how present it all feels. He says he knows logically that the relationship is over, but his body does not seem to know it. He startles easily, sleeps lightly, and feels on edge from the moment he unlocks the shop in the morning. He keeps replaying specific moments—the first slap, the look on her face before she lunged, the sound of objects hitting the wall—as though his mind cannot stop searching them for a way he could have prevented what happened. He feels detached with his current partner, wanting closeness but also flinching from raised voices, sudden movements, even ordinary disagreements. What troubles him most is the sense that he is no longer fully inside his own life. He goes through the motions of opening the shutters, stocking shelves, greeting customers, and closing the till, while underneath he is still listening for danger.
